citations.quote: The Department of Education (DepEd) says there is still work to be done, citing feedback from employers who find some senior high school graduates not yet sufficiently prepared for the workplace.
Education Secretary Sonny Angara said DepEd is looking to increase the amount of on-the-job training (OJT) for senior high school students to 640 hours, from the current 80 to 160 hours.

(That’s the feedback we’ve received from many employers—that the senior high graduates they hire seem to still be unprepared and are not yet accustomed to an eight-hour workday.) With this, Angara said one of DepEd’s interventions is to increase the time learners spend in actual workplaces.
“So some of the interventions, aligned also na rin sa instruction ng ating mahal na Pangulo, is to increase the on-the-job training, or the number of hours spent in workplaces," he said.

(So some of the interventions, also aligned with the instruction of our President, are to increase on-the-job training, or the number of hours spent in workplaces.) “So doon sa mga employers, to any industries to absorb ang learners na po natin, ay ang goal natin is umakyat sa 640 hours of on-the-job training, kumpara doon sa ngayon 80 to 160," Angara added.

(So for employers, for any industries that will absorb our learners, our goal is to increase [the requirement] to 640 hours of on-the-job training, compared with the current 80 to 160.) Angara noted that some employers already provide as much as 500 hours, but consultations with industry groups showed that employers wanted longer workplace exposure to assess students’ fitness for work and help develop their skills.
He added that longer OJT could also improve graduates’ chances of being hired by the same employers who trained them.

“At ang kagandahan niyan, pag nakilala na ho talaga ng employer, mas malaki na ho yung chance na siya ay ma-hire pagka-graduate niya dahil nag-invest na rin sa training yung employer na nag-employ sa kanya as an on-the-job trainee," he said.
